notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Nehemiah 5, drawing on the sources I was able to access.

---

## Nehemiah 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

The chapter shifts from *external* opposition (ch. 4, from Sanballat and Tobiah) to an *internal* crisis — economic exploitation among fellow Jews. Nehemiah confronts wealthy nobles who are charging usury and forcing the poor into debt-slavery, then models servant-leadership by refusing the governor’s allowance for twelve years.

---

### v. 1: *“About that time there was a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews.”*

The chapter opens with a “great outcry” (*tse‘āqâ*, the same word used in Exodus 3:7 for the cry Israel made under Egyptian oppression and in Genesis 18:21 for the outcry against Sodom). Bob Utley (cited at Precept Austin) notes this term is commonly used of an outcry heard by God, often in a legal sense — here it is a cry against fellow Jews, not foreign oppressors.

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

Ellicott observes that Nehemiah’s troubles had previously come from enemies without; now he “begins this account by laying emphasis on the hard treatment of Jews by Jews.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that chapter 4 ended on a note of victory, but here there is no mention of work on the wall — the work had stopped because of internal strife.

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 2: *“We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive.”*

This is the first of three distinct groups voicing complaints. This group had large families but no land; they simply needed food to survive. Ellicott calls this a “general appeal for the governor’s help.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

The Believer’s Study Bible (cited at Precept Austin) identifies the three groups: (1) large landless families needing food; (2) those who mortgaged land to buy food; (3) those who borrowed to pay taxes.

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 3: *“We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine.”*

Ellicott notes that “dearth” (KJV) does not refer to a particular famous famine but to their present hunger. Past mortgages had already strained their resources.

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Guzik observes that a famine is no one’s fault; many financial problems are not anyone’s fault — yet there may be a failing in how the problems are addressed. People had money problems because they worked hard on the wall and did not spend the same time providing for their households.

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 4: *“We have borrowed money to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards.”*

These people had taken loans to pay the Persian imperial tax. Ellicott explains: “We have made our fields and vineyards answerable for the payment of the Persian tribute” — they had pledged the coming produce.

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Gill’s Exposition notes that priests, Levites, and Nethinims were exempt from this tax, but not the common people. Some were so poor they could not pay without borrowing on their estates and paying large usury.

[https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/5.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/5.htm)

Guzik notes these taxes were not the fault of the people; neither Nehemiah nor the people acted as if the taxes were unfair — yet they were still a hardship. He also points out that government kept taxing even though people weren’t working as much and the cost of living went up.

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 5: *“We and our children are just like our countrymen and their children, yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery… we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others.”*

The climax of the outcry: parents forced to sell their children, especially daughters, into servitude. Ellicott notes they had been “obliged to sell until the Jubile for money: children as precious to their parents as were the children of the rulers to them.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

The phrase “our flesh is as the flesh of our brethren” is a plea for equality — the poor are no different from the rich, yet their children are being enslaved while the wealthy suffer nothing. Ryrie (cited at Precept Austin) notes that some daughters were “already enslaved,” and the root problem was that the land (their means of income) was in the hands of others, making redemption impossible.

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 6: *“When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry.”*

Nehemiah’s anger was not rash — it was a *righteous* response to injustice within the covenant community. Guzik says Nehemiah became angry because (a) greed violated the Law of Moses (Exodus 22:25), (b) it fractured the unity of God’s people, and (c) it stopped the work on the walls.

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

Steven Cole (cited at Precept Austin) notes: “The Bible clearly teaches that most anger is sinful, but that some anger is righteous (Eph. 4:26, 31). Jesus got angry at the hardness of heart of the Pharisees (Mark 3:5), but He did not sin. If our anger is directed against the sinful treatment of others and if we allow it to move us toward constructive means to try to resolve the problem, it may be righteous anger.”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

Ellicott adds that Nehemiah, recently arrived, had not known this state of things before the outcry.

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

---

### v. 7: *“After serious thought I rebuked the nobles and officials, saying, ‘You are exacting usury from your own brothers!’ So I called a large assembly against them.”*

This is a key verse on leadership. Guzik says: “He was a man passionate enough to get angry; but wise enough to not act until he had considered the matter carefully.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

Ellicott notes that Nehemiah “mastered himself, and studied his plan of operation. The matter was complicated, as the transgressors had violated rather the spirit than the letter of the law. Hence the rebuke … failed in its object; and the governor called a general assembly, not ‘against them,’ but ‘concerning them.’”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Cole (Precept Austin) notes that Nehemiah likely followed the pattern of private confrontation before public: “First, he privately confronted those guilty of mistreating the poor (Neh 5:7). … Did Nehemiah succeed in private? We don’t know for sure, but probably not. There is no recorded response from the nobles at this point.”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 8: *“We have done our best to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to foreigners, but now you are selling your own brothers, that they may be sold back to us!” But they remained silent, for they could find nothing to say.*

Ellicott calls this “a strong appeal.” Nehemiah and his friends had redeemed Jews from the heathen with money; these men had caused Jews to be sold to *Jews*. “They might have replied had the letter of the law been urged; but this argument puts them to shame.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

The Ligonier devotional notes: “In sum, many wealthy Jews misused the law of God, with the result that many poor Jews were on the verge of entering into perpetual slavery.”

[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/nehemiah-rescues-the-poor](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/nehemiah-rescues-the-poor)

Guzik: “Nehemiah noted that when Judah was conquered, many Jews were sold as slaves to foreigners and many of them had been bought out of slavery by other Jews. Because of this, it was very wrong to have Jews being sold into slavery to other Jews.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 9: *“What you are doing is not right. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?”*

The fear of God is the theological root of the problem. Ellicott notes that Nehemiah 6 shows how watchful the heathen were; “every act of oppression would become a reproach against the God of the Jews.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

**Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** The devotional centres on this verse (“Coram Deo”): “God’s law is given to redeemed people as a delight (Ps. 119:97). When people use the law to put burdens on us that cannot be fulfilled, the law is being used improperly. Nehemiah worked to apply the law properly and ease the burden on the poor, as the law was intended to do.”

[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/nehemiah-rescues-the-poor](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/nehemiah-rescues-the-poor)

**Baptist/Reformed-Baptist perspective (Desiring God):** In a 2024 article, Desiring God zeroes in on the fear of God: “The people are mistreating one another because they don’t really know God. … When there’s no fear of God — no awe of his sovereignty, no respect of his power, no grasp of his will … then there’s no basis for us to truly love others.” The article connects it to Leviticus 25:35–43 where the commands not to charge interest and not to enslave are both tied to the rationale “but fear your God.”

[https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/doctrine-matters-for-deeds-of-mercy](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/doctrine-matters-for-deeds-of-mercy)

---

### v. 10: *“I, as well as my brothers and my servants, have been lending the people money and grain. Please, let us stop this usury.”*

Ellicott translates this differently from the KJV tradition: “We have lent them money and corn. By his own example the governor pleads with them: not ‘let us leave off this usury,’ but let us all and together ‘remit the loans.’”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Some commentators think Nehemiah is admitting his own past failure in lending at interest (because of the plural “let us stop”). Steven Cole disagrees: “Nehemiah had loaned money in accordance with the Law, without charging interest. He is appealing to these wealthy men to join him in doing the same.”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 11: *“Please restore to them immediately their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses, along with the percentage of the money, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been assessing them.”*

The “percentage” / “hundredth part” is understood by most commentators as 1% per month, or 12% annual interest. Ellicott: “The monthly payment of one per cent. per month, twelve per cent. in the year, they were required to give up for the future.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Guzik: “Nehemiah was not asking the nobles and the rulers to just feel bad, or to just stop what they were doing; they had to set the wrong they had done right. If money had been charged unfairly or collateral was taken unfairly, it had to be set right.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 12: *“‘We will restore it,’ they replied, ‘and will require nothing more from them. We will do as you say.’ So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath that they would do what they had promised.”*

The nobles and rulers responded with remarkable teachability. Guzik: “Their teachable spirit, open to correction, was impressive; too few are willing to admit they are wrong and to do what is right – especially if money is involved.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

Ellicott notes that Nehemiah required an oath “to give legal validity to the procedure, and the priests’ presence gave it the highest religious sanction.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

---

### v. 13: *“I also shook out the folds of my robe and said, ‘May God likewise shake out of His house and possession every man who does not keep this promise…’ The whole assembly said, ‘Amen,’ and they praised the LORD.”*

This is a prophetic symbolic act. Ellicott: “This symbolical act imprecated on every man who broke this covenant an appropriate penalty: that he be emptied of all his possessions, even as the fold of Nehemiah’s garment was emptied. And it is observable that the iniquity thus stopped is not referred to in the subsequent covenant (Nehemiah 10), nor is it one of the offences which the governor found on his second return (Nehemiah 13).”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Cole (Precept Austin): “Nehemiah knew that human nature is full of good intentions that never make it into practice. So he made these rich men take a public oath before the priests, that they would follow through. … Surprisingly, no one said, ‘Don’t you trust us?’”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 14: *“Furthermore, from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me to be their governor in the land of Judah, from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total), neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor.”*

This begins Nehemiah’s personal testimony. Ellicott notes: “The whole narrative, thus far, was written after his return from Jerusalem, and on a review of his governorship. … At the close of the twelve years’ term, Nehemiah could say that he and his official attendants had not drawn the customary allowances from the people.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Guzik: “Nehemiah was a great example of putting the work of God ahead of his own personal interest. He certainly had the right to tax the people for his support (others had done it before him), but he didn’t claim that right because it wouldn’t help the work of God.” He draws a parallel to the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:1–15.

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 15: *“The governors before me had heavily burdened the people… But I did not do this, because of my fear of God.”*

Ellicott notes that former governors received bread, wine, and forty shekels of silver — “about four pounds from the entire people daily.” Nehemiah contrasts his forbearance with the conduct of former governors; “we cannot suppose him to mean Zerubbabel, but some of his successors. The practice he condemns was common among the satraps of the Persian princes.” He also observes: “Note that usury and rigour were interdicted, in Leviticus 25:36; Leviticus 25:43, with the express sanction, ‘Fear thy God.’”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Guzik: “Nehemiah could say this because it didn’t matter to him what others did, how the crowd acted, and what the rest of the world thought. He lived by another standard.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

---

### v. 16: *“Instead, I devoted myself to the construction of the wall, and all my servants were gathered there for the work; we did not acquire any land.”*

Ellicott: “His servants and himself did not take advantage of the people’s poverty to acquire their land by mortgage; they were, on the contrary, absorbed in the common work.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Cole (Precept Austin) notes: “Nehemiah and his servants probably knew in advance that real estate prices would shoot up once the wall was completed. They could have bought up land cheaply before announcing the project and then sold the land at a tidy profit. But the soldier in active service does not get entangled in everyday affairs, so that he may please the one who enlisted him (2 Tim. 2:4).”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 17: *“There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, besides the guests from the surrounding nations.”*

Ellicott: “The charge on the governor’s free hospitality was heavy: ‘of the Jews a hundred and fifty rulers, besides those that came’ occasionally from the country.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

---

### v. 18: *“Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and some fowl were prepared for me, and once every ten days an abundance of all kinds of wine was provided. But I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy.”*

Guzik: “Nehemiah not only did not take when he could have; he also gave when he didn’t have to. He received a lot of food from the king’s provisions, which he could have sold for his own profit. Instead, he gave them away to be the example of generosity — feeding as many as 150 people regularly.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

Cole adds: he “feared God and cared about hurting people (Neh 5:15b, 18b). … ‘because the servitude was heavy on this people’ (Neh 5:18b). Every man in leadership must constantly remember that he is only a servant under God.”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

### v. 19: *“Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people.”*

This is Nehemiah’s personal prayer, not for human applause but for divine remembrance. Ellicott: “Nehemiah humbly asks his recompense not from them, but from God. Nothing was more distant from his thoughts than the fame of his good deeds.”

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

Guzik addresses the objection that Nehemiah was boasting: “Jesus clearly taught us that our good works must not be done to show others how spiritual we are (Matt. 6:1–4). But in his prayer, Nehemiah did not look for praise from man — but from God. In fact, Nehemiah probably originally intended that no one else see all or part of this book, because it was written as a diary. … It is entirely appropriate — and right — to say, ‘Remember me, my God, for good’ — to have confidence in our heavenly reward, instead of the praise of men.”

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

Cole cites Matthew Henry: “He mentions it to God in prayer not as if he thought he had hereby merited any favor from God, as a debt, but to show that he looked not for any recompense of his generosity from men, but depended upon God only.”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier)
The Ligonier devotional emphasises the *proper use of God’s law*. The wealthy Jews “misused the law of God” — the law permitted collateral and indentured servitude in ordinary times, but these were not ordinary times. The law’s *intent* was to protect the poor, not create perpetual poverty. Nehemiah’s sacrifice exceeded the letter of the law. The “Coram Deo” application: “God’s law is given to redeemed people as a delight … we will be able to apply the law properly only if we seek God’s wisdom and study the law carefully for its intent and right application.”

[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/nehemiah-rescues-the-poor](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/nehemiah-rescues-the-poor)

### Baptist / Reformed Baptist (Desiring God)
Desiring God frames the entire chapter as a *theological collapse* — the people do not fear God, and that is why they exploit each other. The problem is not merely economic but doctrinal: “How we treat others is always determined by what we think about God.” The article concludes with a Christ-centred gospel turn: “God will have a people who care for their poor brothers because God himself actually became our poor brother to care for us” (2 Cor. 8:9). The chapter becomes a pointer to the New Covenant, where God writes His law on hearts (Jer. 31:34).

[https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/doctrine-matters-for-deeds-of-mercy](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/doctrine-matters-for-deeds-of-mercy)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik’s application focuses heavily on *practical leadership* and *personal example*. Nehemiah models righteous anger under self-control, direct confrontation, personal sacrifice, and accountability structures. Guzik also draws an application about ministers and money: “There’s something wrong with a minister who will only minister to God’s people if the money is right.” The prayer in v. 19 is read as affirming confidence in heavenly reward — a theme that resonates with charismatic emphasis on personal relationship with God.

[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-5/)

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott (1878) provides the most detailed historical-grammatical reading. He is careful on textual nuance: the “great assembly” was “concerning them” not “against them”; the “hundredth part” is 1% monthly and is to be given up *for the future*; Nehemiah’s personal account was written after the twelve-year term. His reading emphasises that the nobles had “violated rather the spirit than the letter of the law” — a characteristically Anglican concern for both law and equity.

[https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/5.htm)

### Broad Evangelical / Non-Denominational (Precept Austin / Steven Cole / Bob Utley)
Precept Austin compiles multiple sources. Bob Utley notes the legal dimension of the “outcry.” The Believer’s Study Bible takes the view that Nehemiah “does not appear to have charged the lenders with lawbreaking” — the language of “usury” in vv. 7 and 10 may simply mean lending against a pledge, not charging interest per se. Steven Cole structures the whole passage around five principles for biblical conflict resolution in the church, from “people must air complaints to the proper authorities” to “leaders must require accountability.”

[https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-5-commentary)

---

## What I Could Not Find

- **Catholic / Orthodox readings:** My search and fetch limits were reached before I could access newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for their specific treatments of Nehemiah 5.
- **Lutheran sources (LCMS / 1517.org) and Methodist/Wesleyan sources (Seedbed):** Not reached within my search limits.
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey):** Not accessed.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / hyper-grace readings:** No results from the approved sites addressed these traditions specifically on this chapter.

The notes above are limited to the sources I was able to reach within the tool-use constraints.
